headline: After a brief lull Wednesday, another strong storm arrives Wednesday night into Thanksgiving with wind advisories from the Strait of Juan de Fuca to Seattle, more heavy rain, and widespread coastal flooding at Thursday's high tides, so expect slow holiday travel along I-5.

sections.title: Today & Tonight
sections.text: Rain is falling Tuesday evening mainly over the Olympic Peninsula and the east side of Puget Sound and moving north to northeast, while parts of Thurston, Lewis and Pierce counties are mostly dry with only a stray shower. Rain is mostly coming down at about a tenth of an inch per hour, up to a quarter inch per hour in spots east of the Sound and up to half an inch per hour on the southwest slopes of the Olympics, with some heavy bands overnight as the front pushes inland. It was unusually mild Tuesday, with Bellingham and Sea-Tac setting record highs by a degree, so snow stays confined to the high mountains; a Winter Weather Advisory for the Whatcom and Skagit Cascades and a Wind Advisory for the coast and western and southern Olympic foothills both end at 10 PM. Winds ease across Puget Sound overnight but stay gusty around the Strait of Juan de Fuca, the San Juans and the coast.

sections.title: Short Term
sections.text: Wednesday brings showers and somewhat lighter, more southerly winds before the next front brings another round of strong south winds late Wednesday night into Thursday. Wind Advisories run 4 PM Wednesday to 11 AM Thursday for the Eastern and Western Strait of Juan de Fuca (Sequim and Port Angeles), Port Townsend, the Lake Crescent/US 101 area, the San Juans, Island County, Everett, the Skagit and Whatcom lowlands and the coast, and 8 PM Wednesday to noon Thursday for Seattle, the Eastside, Kitsap, Tacoma, Olympia, Hood Canal and the Olympics; gusts of roughly 45–50 mph are expected through Puget Sound (40–45 mph at Sea-Tac) and 50–55 mph or more on the coast, with winds staying up much of Thursday, so allow extra travel time, especially on I-5. The ongoing rain adds another 2–5 inches across the region, most in the Olympics, with a slight chance of thunderstorms Thursday after the front; a Flood Watch runs Wednesday morning through Sunday afternoon for the Olympics and their western and southern foothills, Olympia and southern Puget Sound, southern Hood Canal, the Chehalis Valley and the Willapa and Black Hills, where the Skokomish River in Mason County should reach moderate flooding midweek, though no widespread river flooding is expected. In the North Cascades, a Winter Storm Watch late Wednesday night through Thursday afternoon calls for up to 15 inches of snow at Washington Pass and above 5,000 feet.

sections.title: Long Term
sections.text: Things settle somewhat Friday, and Saturday should be a brief break from rain for most of the area. More storms are forecast from Sunday on as low pressure returns offshore, keeping the weather active into early December.

coast: Tuesday's coastal flooding did significant damage along the Pacific coast, and waves there can throw large rocks and logs ashore, so stay off jetties and the immediate shoreline; a High Surf Advisory covers the north and Grays Harbor coasts until 4 PM Wednesday. Wednesday morning's high tides bring a Coastal Flood Warning 3–10 AM for San Juan County and a Coastal Flood Advisory 2–9 AM for the Seattle, Everett, Kitsap, Island County, Port Townsend, northern Hood Canal, Pierce/south King, Skagit/Snohomish and Whatcom shorelines, then a Coastal Flood Warning 9 AM–4 PM for the Eastern and Western Strait of Juan de Fuca (Sequim, Port Angeles) and the north and Grays Harbor coasts, plus an advisory for the lower Chehalis Valley. Even higher tides arrive Thursday together with the next front: a Coastal Flood Watch runs late Wednesday night through Thursday afternoon for nearly all of those shorelines including the Strait, with major flooding possible at Friday Harbor, Westport and Cherry Point and moderate flooding at the other tide gauges. The threat eases slightly Friday, but longer-range models hint that weekend low pressure could bring it back. Seas of 15–25 feet stay up through midday Wednesday, ease to 10–15 feet by Thursday afternoon and 6–9 feet Saturday and Sunday, then build above 10 feet Monday. For boaters, a Storm Warning covers the coastal waters until 1 AM Wednesday, then a Gale Warning until 1 PM, then another Storm Warning 1–10 PM Wednesday with slightly stronger winds than Tuesday's storm; the east Strait has a Gale Warning until 10 PM Wednesday, the west Strait a Small Craft Advisory until 1 PM then a Gale Warning 1–10 PM Wednesday, and the northern inland waters and San Juans a Gale Warning until 5 AM Wednesday then a Small Craft Advisory to 10 PM, while the central Strait gets an overnight lull (Small Craft Advisory until 10 PM Tuesday). Small Craft Advisories also cover Puget Sound and Hood Canal until 10 AM Wednesday and Admiralty Inlet and the Grays Harbor bar until 10 PM Wednesday; isolated thunderstorms are possible over the coastal waters each afternoon and evening through Thursday, and high pressure should bring a brief break from the wind Friday before winds pick up again next week.
watch_for: Coastal flooding at Thursday's high tides, possibly major at Friday Harbor, Westport and Cherry Point and moderate along the Strait of Juan de Fuca and Puget Sound.
Strong south winds late Wednesday night into Thursday that could slow Thanksgiving travel along I-5.
The Skokomish River's rise to moderate flooding midweek, and whether weekend low pressure brings coastal flooding back.
confidence: Forecasters say the existing forecast and warnings still match the latest computer models for the stormy round Wednesday night into Thursday, while the weekend's possible return of coastal flooding and the timing of next week's storms rest on less certain longer-range guidance.
